approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Blue Lake Trailhead on the south side of SR-20, roughly 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass, at about 5,200 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required and the lot is small enough that it fills on summer weekends.

Walk the maintained Blue Lake Trail for about a mile and a half. The turnoff is a signed junction — the sign points straight on for Blue Lake and left for Liberty Bell Trail #727, Climbing Access — and it sits just past a small stream in a meadow, with a large cairn beside it. That stream is the last water you can count on.

Trail #727 climbs hard through granite slabs, talus and heather benches toward the gully that drains the notch between Liberty Bell and Concord Tower. In the gully itself the loose ground is least bad if you keep to climber's left for the lower two thirds, then cross and hug climber's right for the rest. Where the boot path forks a couple of hundred feet below the notch, take the left branch; the right branch leads on toward Lexington and Concord's south side.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Do not start climbing from the notch itself. The first pitch begins from a tree standing roughly 30 feet BELOW the crest of the Liberty Bell-Concord notch, on the Liberty Bell (north) side. From that tree a small ledge runs left; walk it and it delivers you to the foot of a blocky chimney, and that chimney is pitch one. If you are stood on the low point of the notch looking for a crack going straight up, you are too high and too far right — drop back down to the tree. Concord Tower's North Face starts from the top of the same notch, on the opposite (south) wall, so two parties can be at the same notch climbing in opposite directions; check which wall you are facing before you rack up.
hazards: loose rock and party-induced rockfall in the notch gully — helmets on before entering, and avoid stacking up under other parties
steep 3rd-class steps on the climbers' path when wet
trailhead lot fills early on summer weekends; roadside parking on SR-20 is limited

approach_variants.name: Early-season snow gully to the notch
approach_variants.season: Highway opening (typically mid-late Apr or early May) through late Jun
approach_variants.notes:
The same line as the summer approach, but the upper gully below the Liberty Bell-Concord notch commonly holds snow into late June and the boot path through the slabs and heather may be buried lower down. Parties carry an ice axe, and crampons if the snow has refrozen overnight.

SR-20 over Washington and Rainy Passes is gated every winter — it typically closes in late November or early December and reopens somewhere between mid-April and early May, with the exact dates set by snowpack and avalanche conditions rather than a calendar. Until the gate opens there is no drive-up access to the Blue Lake Trailhead at all.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Snow changes what the last hundred metres looks like. With the gully filled, the notch reads as a clean snow finish rather than a scree saddle, and the tree that marks the Beckey start — about 30 feet below the crest on the Liberty Bell side, with a small ledge running left to the blocky chimney — can be partly buried or standing above a moat. If you top out onto the notch crest and find no tree, you have gone above the start; downclimb the last stretch on the Liberty Bell side and look for it. Expect a moat where snow pulls away from the rock at the base of the chimney.
hazards: firm or refrozen snow in the gully — a slip runs a long way over rock
moat at the transition from snow to rock at the base of the first pitch
wet-loose and cornice debris in the gully during spring melt
SR-20 gated in winter — no vehicle access to the trailhead until the highway reopens

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch (traverse start)
approach_variants.notes:
The traverse starts by climbing Liberty Bell, so the walk in is the Beckey Route approach: Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,200 ft) on SR-20 about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass, a mile and a half of maintained Blue Lake Trail to the signed Liberty Bell Trail #727 climbing-access junction just past a small stream and marked by a large cairn, then Trail #727 up slabs, talus and heather to the gully below the Liberty Bell-Concord notch (~7,300 ft).

Because the traverse ends on South Early Winters Spire and descends that peak's South Arete line back into the same Blue Lake basin, no car shuttle is needed — the whole link-up is a loop from one trailhead. Keep to climber's left in the lower gully and cross to the right side higher up; take the left fork of the boot path a couple of hundred feet below the notch.
approach_variants.baseFinding: The traverse's first climbing is the Beckey Route, so the start is the same tree about 30 feet below the crest of the Liberty Bell-Concord notch on the Liberty Bell side, with a short ledge running left to a blocky chimney. From the notch you can also see the whole rest of the day's line to the south: Concord Tower's wall immediately opposite, then Lexington, then the two Early Winters Spires beyond. If you cannot see that stepped southward skyline from where you are stood, you are in the wrong notch.
hazards: rockfall in the notch gully, made worse by the number of parties using it
long committing link-up with no easy bail once past Concord
lingering snow in the notch gully into late June

approach_variants.name: East Face from the SR-20 hairpin pullout
approach_variants.notes:
This route is on the east side of the mountain and is NOT approached from the Blue Lake Trailhead. Drive to the hairpin turn on SR-20 a short way east of Washington Pass and park in the turnout there.

Walk back along the road toward the pass until you see the small pond on the south side of the highway. The boot path starts at the pond's east end and goes north into the timber; it is cairned, but the cairns are easy to lose in the dark on a pre-dawn start, so scout the first few minutes in daylight the evening before if you can.

The path climbs steeply through forest and then breaks out onto the talus directly under the East Face. Reported times run from about half an hour to roughly three quarters of an hour of steep walking. There is no water on this approach — carry it from the car.

One consequence worth planning for: if you continue to the true summit and take the standard notch descent, you come down on the WEST side of the mountain and will need a shuttle or a road walk back to the hairpin. Most parties instead rappel the East Face and return directly to their packs.
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the talus, Liberty Crack is the obvious continuous vertical crack that passes to the RIGHT of the huge roof high on the wall — the roof is the Lithuanian Lip, and it is the single feature that identifies the line even in flat light. Do not scramble straight up beneath it. The standard entry traverses in from the LEFT for roughly 40 feet on third- and fourth-class ledges to reach the ledges directly under the true first-pitch crack; there is also a fourth-class alternative that goes up the right-hand side of the block at the base. Parties that head straight up the fall line from the talus end up on the neighbouring East Face lines rather than on Liberty Crack — the East Face here holds a whole cluster of routes within a few rope lengths of each other, so pick the line by the roof above you, not by whichever crack is nearest.
hazards: loose talus and boulders at the base of the wall
cairned forest path is genuinely hard to follow before dawn
no water between the car and the wall
rockfall from parties on the East Face routes above

approach_variants.name: Early-season snow and moat at the East Face base
approach_variants.season: Late spring / early summer after the highway opens, while snow still covers the talus
approach_variants.notes:
Same trailhead and same cairned path from the pond's east end, but early in the season the talus under the wall is buried in snow that firms up hard overnight. Parties have reported chipping steps in icy snow to reach the rock, and finding the snow lying steeply enough that a slip would carry you a long way down the slope.

Carry an axe and traction, and expect to be in boots for the walk in even when the wall itself is dry.
approach_variants.baseFinding: The identifier is still the big roof — Liberty Crack is the continuous crack running past the right side of the Lithuanian Lip. What changes is the last few metres: a deep moat opens where the snow pulls away from the base of the wall, and getting from snow into the rock can mean a committing step across or a short stemming move down and back up out of the gap. Scout along the base rather than dropping into the first moat you meet; parties have found the moat mellowing out within about thirty feet of where they first reached it.
hazards: deep moat between snow and rock at the base of the wall
hard refrozen snow over talus — a slip runs out badly
SR-20 is gated all winter, so this window only opens once the highway reopens (typically mid-late April to early May)

approach_variants.name: East Face from the SR-20 hairpin pullout
approach_variants.notes:
Shared with every route on this wall: park at the hairpin turnout on SR-20 just east of Washington Pass, walk back west along the shoulder to the small pond on the south side of the road, round its east end, and follow the cairned boot path north into the trees. It climbs steeply through timber and comes out on the talus directly beneath the East Face in roughly half an hour to an hour.

No water on the way. The cairns are hard to follow in the dark.

If you finish on the true summit and descend the standard west-side notch line you will be about a mile of highway from your car, so plan a shuttle or accept the road walk.
approach_variants.baseFinding: The East Face carries a dense cluster of routes in a short stretch of wall, so identify your line off the big features before you leave the talus rather than by picking the nearest crack. The reference point everybody uses is the large roof high on the left-hand part of the wall — the Lithuanian Lip — which Liberty Crack passes on its right. Anything you start well right of that roof-and-crack system is a different route. Approach ledges at the base are third and fourth class and traverse in from the left, so the start of a line is usually a short sideways walk from where the talus meets the rock, not straight up from it.
hazards: loose talus at the base
cairned path easy to lose before dawn
rockfall from parties higher on the wall
descent by the west-side notch leaves you at the wrong trailhead

wa_liberty_bell_east_face._note: Only the shared East Face walk-in is recorded. No source found that pins the individual start of this particular East Face line among the cluster, so no route-specific baseFinding is claimed.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to the Beckey Route walk-in, which is why the two are so often climbed on the same day. Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,200 ft) on SR-20 about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass; a mile and a half of maintained trail to the signed Liberty Bell Trail #727 climbing-access junction just past a small stream, marked with a large cairn; then the climbers' path up slabs, talus and heather into the bowl below the towers and up the gully to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at about 7,300 ft.

In the gully, staying climber's left for the lower two thirds and then crossing to climber's right keeps you on the most stable ground.
approach_variants.baseFinding: The route starts AT the top of the notch, on the Concord (south) side — not below it. Stand on the crest of the Liberty Bell-Concord col and turn to face Concord Tower: the first pitch is the crack system running up that wall to a large ledge holding a few small trees, and that ledge is the pitch-one belay and is visible from the notch. The mistake to avoid is dropping 30 feet down the Liberty Bell side to the tree with the ledge running left into a blocky chimney — that is the Beckey Route on Liberty Bell, the other tower, and parties heading for opposite summits share this saddle all day. If your first pitch tops out on a treed ledge you are on Concord; if it starts by walking a small ledge leftward into a chimney you are on Liberty Bell.
hazards: loose, heavily trafficked gully below the notch — helmets, and don't queue underneath another party
hollow-sounding flakes on the upper pitches send debris to the notch
no water above the stream at the Trail #727 junction

approach_variants.name: Early-season snow to the notch
approach_variants.notes:
Same line, but the gully feeding the Liberty Bell-Concord notch holds snow into late June most years and the boot path lower down may still be buried. Ice axe standard, crampons if it has refrozen.

One upside of the early season here: while the gully is snow-filled the rock in it is locked in place, and rockfall gets noticeably worse once it melts out.

SR-20 is closed across Washington Pass every winter, typically from late November or early December until mid-April to early May, so this window begins whenever the highway reopens.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Snow does not move the start — it is still the crack system on the Concord wall rising directly from the crest of the notch to the treed ledge. What snow does is fill the notch, so the col reads as a smooth saddle and the base of the first pitch can sit above a moat. Look up at the tower on the south side of the col for the treed ledge to confirm you are on the right wall before committing.
hazards: firm snow in the gully with a long runout below
moat between snow and rock at the base
SR-20 gated in winter — no vehicle access until the highway reopens

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Concord-Lexington notch
approach_variants.notes:
The South Face is reached from the notch between Concord and Lexington, which is a different saddle from the Liberty Bell-Concord notch that the North Face and the Beckey Route use. From the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,200 ft, about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass) follow the maintained trail until it opens out, then take the well-established climbers' path on the left marked by a large cairn.

Instead of trending toward the Liberty Bell-Concord gully, keep working up and left into the gully between Concord and Lexington Towers. Higher in that gully a reasonable climbers' path appears along its LEFT side; take it rather than fighting up the gully bed. It leads to the Concord-Lexington notch.

This notch is the quieter of the two — it sees far less traffic than the Liberty Bell-Concord col.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You want the Concord-Lexington notch, meaning the saddle with Concord Tower on one side and Lexington Tower on the other. From it, the South Face is on the Concord (north) side, and it begins gently: a class-2 walk across gravelly, slightly down-sloping ledges gets you to the first belay, so if your first move is a hard pull you are on the wrong line. Higher, a roped scramble along the crest brings you to a sandy stance under a thin blade of rock that climbers call the shark fin, and the last pitch goes over that fin onto the summit block, belaying from bolts. The shark fin is the confirming feature — it is unmistakable and there is nothing like it on the North Face side.

The common error is arriving at the Liberty Bell-Concord notch instead. That col has Liberty Bell on its far side, not Lexington, and from there the Concord wall in front of you is the North Face crack system, not walkable ledges.
hazards: loose ground in the Concord-Lexington gully
easy to end up in the Liberty Bell-Concord gully instead — check which two towers flank your notch
no reliable water above the stream near the climbers'-path junction

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail and the Concord-Lexington gully
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,200 ft) on SR-20 roughly 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass. Follow the maintained Blue Lake Trail until the terrain opens up — around a mile and a half to two miles — and pick up the well-established climbers' path branching left at a large cairn.

From there, trend LEFT of the line most parties take toward the Liberty Bell-Concord notch, and work up into the gully that separates Lexington Tower from Concord Tower. As you gain height in that gully a decent boot path shows up along its left side; use it. It brings you to the Concord-Lexington col.

Carry water from the trailhead. Snowmelt trickles low in the basin dry up by mid-summer.
approach_variants.baseFinding: The route does not start from the high point of the col. From the crest, move slightly WEST and drop a couple of feet: the first pitch begins at an obvious slanting, right-leaning crack in the Lexington side of the notch, and the 5.7 crux is the very first thing you climb — awkward moves straight off the ground. Follow the leaning crack for about 15 to 20 feet and it eases into stemming up a chimney at around 5.6. If your first moves are easy you are probably on the Concord wall opposite, which is the South Face of Concord and starts by walking gravelly ledges rather than pulling on a crack. A hard start on a right-leaning crack, just below and west of the col, is the confirmation.
hazards: loose rock in the Concord-Lexington gully
lingering firm snow or névé in the upper gully into early summer — axe or traction useful
the descent uses slung horns rather than fixed anchors, so carry spare webbing

approach_variants.name: Early-season snow to the Concord-Lexington col
approach_variants.notes:
Same approach, but the upper gully to the col commonly holds firm snow into early summer, which buries the boot path along its left side and turns the last stretch into a snow climb. Carry an axe, and crampons if it is refrozen.

SR-20 is gated across Washington Pass through the winter — typically closing in late November or early December and reopening between mid-April and early May — so there is no drive-up access until the highway reopens.
approach_variants.baseFinding: With snow in the col the slanting crack that starts the route can be partly buried, and the couple of feet of drop west from the high point may instead be a step down into a moat. The feature to hold onto is that the start is on the LEXINGTON side, slightly west of and just below the crest, at a right-leaning crack, and the hardest climbing of the first pitch is immediately off the deck. If snow has filled the crack's base, expect to start higher up it than the summer start and to be dealing with wet rock for the first body length.
hazards: firm snow in the gully below the col
moat where snow meets the Lexington wall
SR-20 closed in winter — no vehicle access until reopening

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail, then north along the base of the west side
approach_variants.notes:
Nearly all the routes on North Early Winters Spire are on its west side, so the Blue Lake Trailhead is the right side of the mountain to start from — the hairpin pullout on the east serves the East Buttress and couloir lines, not this one.

From the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,200 ft) on SR-20 about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass, follow the maintained trail for roughly a mile and a half to the signed Liberty Bell Trail #727 climbing-access junction, which sits just past a small stream and is marked with a large cairn. That stream is your last reliable water.

Trail #727 switchbacks up slabs, talus and heather into the basin under the west faces. Approach as if for South Early Winters Spire and then traverse LEFT (north) along the base of the formations, scrambling, until you are under North Early Winters Spire. Most parties report one to two hours from the car.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Keep traversing north along the base past the start of the West Face route. The Northwest Corner begins at a distinct corner-and-crack system whose first pitch — around 45 metres of 5.8, including a short chimney section with sparse gear — runs up to a broad ledge covered in trees. That treed ledge is the landmark: it is visible from below and from across the basin, it is the top of pitch one, and the route continues up and left off its left-hand edge. If you are under blank slab with no corner leading to a treed ledge, you have not gone far enough north yet. The corner start is shared with the West Face route, so being at the right corner puts you at the right place for either — the two diverge above the ledge, not below it.
hazards: lingering snow and avalanche debris in the basin and approach gully into June
braided climbers' paths through the upper talus make it easy to drift onto the wrong formation
no water past the stream at the Trail #727 junction
poorly protected chimney section low on the first pitch

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the chasm between the two spires
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,200 ft) on SR-20 about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass, walk the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half to the signed Liberty Bell Trail #727 climbing-access junction just past a small stream and a large cairn, then take the climbers' path up through slabs, talus and heather into the basin below the west faces.

The objective from here is the huge cleft that splits the two Early Winters Spires, seen from the WEST side. Head for its foot. Note this is the west-side gully — the couloir that splits the same two spires on the EAST side, reached from the highway hairpin, is a different feature and a different route.

Be ready to swap between rock shoes and boots if snow is still lying in the gully.
approach_variants.baseFinding: The start is at the very foot of the enormous chasm dividing North from South Early Winters Spire — it is the biggest single feature on this side of the group and it is unambiguous even in poor visibility, because nothing else on the west faces is a full-height cleft between two summits. The route opens with a short step of low-fifth-class slab and layback moves, and then it is walking up the gully bed; if you are pulling on anything hard in the first rope length you are on one of the face routes to either side, not in the gully. Pitch one takes cracks and ramps along the LEFT edge of the gully rather than the middle. The house-sized chockstone that names the route sits much higher up the same gully, so do not expect to see it from the base as your confirmation.
hazards: snow lingering in the gully early season — axe and crampons
loose rock funnelled down the gully, including from parties above
wind in the gully; it channels weather

approach_variants.name: Spire Gully from the SR-20 hairpin (snow)
approach_variants.season: A few weeks right after SR-20 reopens — typically Apr to early May
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the hairpin curve on SR-20 roughly a mile southeast of Washington Pass, directly under the east faces of the two Early Winters Spires. This is the east-side approach; the Blue Lake Trailhead serves the west side and is the wrong side of the mountain for this route.

From the pullout, go straight up Spire Gully on snow. Reports put it at around 1,500 feet of steep snow to the start of the technical ground, and in April that snow can be unconsolidated enough to posthole to the waist — one party described slogging in to the thigh and beyond, while a party on firmer May snow was at the base in under an hour from the car. Time it for a cold night and an early start.

The window is narrow and it is set by the highway. SR-20 across Washington Pass is gated all winter, usually closing late November or early December and reopening between mid-April and early May, and this route is only in condition for a few weeks after that gate opens.
approach_variants.baseFinding: The couloir is the obvious gash splitting the two spires as seen FROM THE HIGHWAY — you can pick it out from the hairpin before you start walking, which is the best moment to fix it in your mind if cloud is forecast. From the top of Spire Gully do not continue straight up into the cleft; traverse NORTH to gain a ramp of snow lying at about 40 degrees, and the technical climbing starts from the TOP of that ramp. The ramp is the handrail: a distinctly moderate-angled snow feature leading leftward into the base of the steeper couloir. Parties that push straight into the cleft from the gully below the ramp are starting too low.
hazards: 1,500 ft of steep snow with avalanche and wet-slide potential on a sun-affected aspect
deep unconsolidated snow early in the window
no fixed anchors in the couloir — a party that retreats down it is improvising anchors on steep broken rock, and a fatal accident occurred this way in 2025
cornice at the top of the couloir
route only exists once SR-20 reopens, and closes out within weeks

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the southwest toe of the spire
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,200 ft) on SR-20 about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass, follow the maintained trail as it climbs through fir and larch and out onto open slabs. After roughly a mile and a quarter to a mile and a half the ground opens up and the Liberty Bell-Concord-Early Winters skyline comes into view; the climbers' track leaves the maintained trail here, at a minor stream draining the basin, sometimes marked with a cairn. This is well short of Blue Lake itself, which is another mile-plus along the maintained trail — if you reach the lake you have gone too far.

The climbers' path works up through granite slabs and heather benches and then up open talus roughly parallel to the stream. The stream is good water low down and vanishes into the talus higher up, so fill there.

Higher, the path loses definition on the talus and slab benches and braids. Rather than chasing one cairn line, navigate to the feature: the southwest corner at the end of the ridge on the right.
approach_variants.baseFinding: You are aiming for the southwest corner — the toe where the south ridge of South Early Winters Spire runs down and ends, which is the right-hand (southernmost) of the two spires, reached before the saddle between them. The arete itself is broad and broken rather than a knife edge, and it separates the Southwest Couloir on its left from the steep East Face on its right; standing at the base you should have the couloir up to one side and steep unclimbable-looking wall to the other. The first pitch begins with a short steep crack; above it you either go right and up across a slab at 5.5 to a small tree, or left across a short friction slab at 5.5. If you are stood at the bottom of a broad snow or scree gully with nothing to climb, you have drifted into the Southwest Couloir and need to move right onto the ridge toe. If you are under steep continuous rock, you have gone too far right onto the east side.
hazards: wet or snow-covered granite slabs low on the climbers' path
braided path and loss of definition on the upper talus
old snow persisting in shaded gullies into early summer
queueing at rappel stations on busy weekends, since this is also the descent line for other routes

approach_variants.name: Early-season, snow in the basin
approach_variants.notes:
The same line in from Blue Lake, but with the basin under snow the climbers' path through the slabs and talus is buried and you are navigating by terrain rather than by boot track. Firm morning snow makes the ascent quicker than summer talus; softening afternoon snow makes the descent slower.

SR-20 across Washington Pass is gated every winter, typically from late November or early December until mid-April to early May, so the season begins when the highway does.
approach_variants.baseFinding: With snow filling the basin the Southwest Couloir is a clean white line and the arete is the rock rib on its right-hand side — that contrast actually makes the toe EASIER to identify than in summer, when couloir and ridge are both grey. Walk up the snow of the couloir's edge and step right onto the rock at the ridge toe, where the short steep crack of the first pitch starts. Expect a moat at the snow-rock junction. Take an axe: the alternative descent down the couloir holds firm snow well into summer.
hazards: moat at the base where snow pulls off the rock
firm snow in the couloir requiring axe and possibly crampons
buried climbers' path — navigate by the couloir and ridge toe, not by cairns
SR-20 gated in winter

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Y-shaped larch
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,200 ft) on SR-20 about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass, walk the maintained trail roughly a mile and a quarter until it opens into a clearing. Leave it at the small stream — often cairned — and follow climbers' tracks up through the slabs alongside the stream into the basin under the west side of the spires.

The meadows here are fragile and heavily used; stay on the established tracks and off the heather.

From the basin, work up the talus toward the west face of South Early Winters Spire, north of the Southwest Couloir.
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base of the route is marked by a larch tree that forks into two trunks in a clear Y — it is the single agreed-upon landmark for this climb and people navigate to it by name. In front of the Y-larch an easy ledge runs up and away from the tree; scramble that ledge and belay off a solid tree, and the first proper pitch follows cracks straight up through an awkward bulge, well protected, to a ledge at the foot of the feature climbers call the Wavy Crack. If you start at a lower or higher point on the rib you skip that first 5.8+ pitch and arrive at the Wavy Crack having missed the best of the lower climbing — so hunt for the Y-larch rather than roping up at whatever looks like the toe. The rib you want is the buttress immediately north of (left of, looking in) the Southwest Couloir.
hazards: fragile alpine meadow crossed by braided tracks — erosion damage and easy to lose the line
loose talus in the basin
shared descent line with South Arete parties, so expect congestion at rappel stations

approach_variants.name: Spire Gully from the SR-20 hairpin (dry)
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the dirt pullout on the obvious hairpin turn on SR-20, directly beneath the east faces of the two Early Winters Spires. Do not use the Blue Lake Trailhead — that is the west-side approach and it puts you on the wrong side of the mountain.

Walk up the obvious gully, which is the easy way through the first band of cliffs above the road. Above that cliff band a faint climbers' path leaves the gully on a gently rising line to the RIGHT, crossing easy slabs and vegetated dirt. Roughly three quarters of an hour out you come to some fourth-class slabs.

The classic sequence of landmarks, and the one to hold in your head: up Spire Gully following occasional cairns to the last big tree in the middle of the gully; from that tree traverse right across talus; that brings you under the gully that runs up to the notch between North and South Early Winters Spires; then traverse left to the foot of the buttress.

The whole line is visible from the road, so look up and read it before you start walking.
approach_variants.baseFinding: The buttress toe is the LOW POINT of the prow, sitting immediately LEFT of the gully that separates North from South Early Winters Spire — so you find it by first locating that dividing gully and then stepping left out of it, rather than by heading straight up from the talus. The first pitch is rambling 5.6 with moss, dirt and some loose rock; a scruffy easy pitch is the correct start here, and if your first pitch is clean and steep you are too high on the buttress or on one of the harder east-side lines. The last large tree in the centre of Spire Gully is the checkpoint before this: if you are still climbing the gully and have passed no such tree, you have not reached the traverse point yet.
hazards: loose rock in Spire Gully, with parties above
fourth-class slabs partway up the approach — a fall there is consequential and unroped
vegetated dirt slopes that are greasy when wet
no water on the approach

approach_variants.name: Early-season, snow in Spire Gully
approach_variants.notes:
Same line from the hairpin, but with snow in Spire Gully the traverse right from the last big tree is done on snow rather than talus. Crampons and an axe are worth carrying; sources on this approach say so explicitly for the early season.

SR-20 is gated over Washington Pass through the winter, typically from late November or early December to mid-April or early May, so this window opens with the highway.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Snow does not move the buttress toe — it is still the low point of the prow just left of the North/South Early Winters dividing gully. What it changes is the traverse: on snow the rightward traverse from the last large tree in the gully is a straightforward but exposed snow crossing rather than a talus scramble, and the transition back onto rock at the base of the buttress will likely involve a moat. Fix the dividing gully visually from the highway before you start — from inside a snowy Spire Gully in flat light the individual features all read the same.
hazards: snow traverse above a runout
moat at the base of the buttress
wet-loose slides off the east faces on a sunny spring day
SR-20 gated in winter

approach_variants.name: Spire Gully from the SR-20 hairpin
approach_variants.notes:
The east-side approach, shared with the other East Buttress lines. Park at the dirt pullout at the hairpin turn on SR-20 beneath the east faces of the Early Winters Spires — not at the Blue Lake Trailhead, which serves the west side.

Go up Spire Gully, which breaches the first cliff band above the road, following occasional cairns. Continue to the last large tree standing in the centre of the gully. From there traverse right across talus, which brings you below the gully leading up to the notch between North and South Early Winters Spires, then traverse back left to the foot of the buttress.

Early season the traverse is on snow rather than talus and an axe and crampons are worth having.
approach_variants.baseFinding: The reference feature is the gully dividing North from South Early Winters Spire. The buttress toe is the low point of the prow immediately LEFT of that gully — locate the gully first, then step left. The last big tree in the middle of Spire Gully is the checkpoint that tells you where to leave the gully and start traversing right; reaching it is what confirms you are far enough up.
hazards: loose rock in Spire Gully
exposed traverse across talus or, early season, snow
no water on the approach

wa_south_early_winter_spire_east_buttres._note: Sources describe the shared East Buttress approach only. This row is not clearly distinguished from the Direct East Buttress in current sources, so nothing route-specific beyond the shared buttress toe is claimed.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail into the west basin (snow)
approach_variants.season: A few weeks to a couple of months after SR-20 reopens — roughly May-Jun
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead on SR-20 about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass, follow the main trail roughly a mile and a half to the well-worn climbers' trail and take it up into the basin on the west side of the Liberty Bell group. Early in the season the trailhead lot itself may still be snowed in.

On a cold morning parties approach in boots and crampons without flotation; later in the day the same snow softens badly. Start early and plan to be off the couloir before the afternoon.

This is the quickest line to the summit of the south spire, and it exists only for a short window: it comes into condition once the highway opens and deteriorates as the snow goes. Late in the season the couloir empties out into loose rock and is not worth climbing.
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the basin, the couloir is the snow gully rising on the southwest side of South Early Winters Spire, immediately left of the South Arete rib as you look up. It broadens low down at a modest 25 to 30 degrees, and the identifying feature is the FORK higher up where the gully splits — the right-hand branch is the route, and it steepens to 40 to 50 degrees and narrows above the split. If you are in a gully that never forks, you are in the wrong drainage. Because the whole thing is a snow feature there is no rock start to find; the transition is simply from basin snow into the gully bed, so the navigational work is choosing the correct gully from the basin, in daylight, before the ground steepens.
hazards: avalanche and wet-slide hazard on a sun-affected slope, worsening through the day
snow and occasional ice to around 50 degrees in the upper narrows
late season the couloir fills with loose rock and becomes a rockfall trap — not recommended once melted out
route depends entirely on SR-20 reopening, typically mid-April to early May

approach_variants.name: State Creek climbers' trail from the SR-20 pullout
approach_variants.notes:
Park in the long pullout on the NORTH side of SR-20 about a mile and a half west of Washington Pass. The trail leaves from the EAST end of that pullout and drops straight into the woods; the climbers' track actually starts on the west side of a clump of trees near the pullout's eastern end and is usually cairned, but it takes some hunting the first time and is easy to walk past.

The path drops through timber, crosses State Creek — fill up, it is the last reliable water — and then climbs steadily up into the big meadow and basin below Cutthroat Peak. Reports put roughly an hour and a half from the car to the foot of the entry gully.

Above the meadow the trail steepens into a boulder field beneath the south buttress.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Standing in the boulder field, several large gullies come down out of the south buttress. Bear RIGHT and take the LEFTMOST of those gullies — that specific choice is the crux of the navigation and it is where parties get it wrong, because from below the gullies look interchangeable.

Climb the gully as scrambling terrain. The place to rope up is not the bottom: continue up until you are about 100 feet from its top, where the gully FORKS and visibly steepens. That fork is the marker. Pitch one goes up the LEFT side of the gully from there to gain the ridge crest. If you rope up down at the base you burn time on ground everybody scrambles; if you find yourself topping out of a gully with no fork and no steepening, you are in the wrong one.
hazards: climbers' trail from the pullout is genuinely hard to find in the dark
State Creek crossing can be awkward in high spring flow
loose rock in the entry gully with parties above
the standard West Ridge descent is looser than the ascent line and has cairned traverses where the direct-looking line cliffs out

approach_variants.name: State Creek approach, continuing low to the buttress toe
approach_variants.notes:
Follow the standard South Buttress approach: the long pullout on the north side of SR-20 about a mile and a half west of Washington Pass, the cairned climbers' track leaving from the east end of it, down through timber, across State Creek (last water), and up into the meadow and basin below the peak.

Where the standard route bears right in the boulder field for the leftmost entry gully, this route instead keeps going lower and further around, leaving the boot path to contour on talus and heather benches to the very bottom of the ridge. That extra contouring is off-trail and adds meaningful distance and gain over the standard walk-in — budget more than the roughly hour-and-a-half everyone quotes for the standard start.
approach_variants.baseFinding: The distinguishing fact about this variation is that it starts BELOW where everyone else does. The correct start is the toe of the lower ridge, on easy ledgy third- and fourth-class slabs, well down and around from the leftmost gully that the standard South Buttress uses. If you are stood at the foot of a steep gully that forks near its top, you are at the standard start and have not gone low enough. The right ground here is unmistakably easy — many rope lengths of ambling slab before anything steepens — so if the first moves feel like real climbing you are too high on the buttress.
hazards: off-trail contouring on talus and heather with no path to follow
much longer day than the standard route for the same summit
dated fixed tat at the two half-rope rappels into notches on the lower ridge

approach_variants.name: State Creek to the basin south of the peak, then the twin gullies
approach_variants.notes:
From the highway, drop to the State Creek crossing as for the South Buttress — the long pullout on the north side of SR-20 about a mile and a half west of Washington Pass, cairned track from its east end down through timber to the creek.

From the creek, climb the open slopes on the EAST side of the southeast-draining stream, which takes you into the basin immediately south of Cutthroat Peak. Reports put roughly an hour and a half to the foot of the gully system.

Continue up to the basin headwall.
approach_variants.baseFinding: At the headwall look for TWIN gullies running up to a notch — that notch is the base of the Southeast Buttress and it is the target. The sequence that matters: start up the RIGHT-hand gully, and traverse across into the LEFT-hand gully BEFORE you reach the notch. Getting that order backwards is the classic error, because from the basin the left gully looks like the direct line. Scramble the lower part of the gully, then rope up and pitch out the upper section to the notch. Above the notch the ground eases to scrambling before a short steep face, and from there you stay near the buttress crest.
hazards: loose rock in both gullies
State Creek crossing in high water
the West Ridge descent option is looser and more rockfall-prone than the ascent line

approach_variants.name: Roadside pullout west of the Blue Lake Trailhead
approach_variants.notes:
There is a broad shoulder with room to park on SR-20 roughly half a mile WEST of the Blue Lake Trailhead, with a view through the trees to the peak. Parties commonly meet at the Blue Lake lot and then drive the short distance west to this pullout.

From there head up into the basin below the peak. Reported round-trip times are on the order of six hours up and four hours down for the whole climb, so this is a long day even though the walk-in is short.

On the way out, the descent line drops skier's right onto a sandy rib with a faint climbers' track, then into another gully further skier's right for the lower part — going straight down instead puts you into loose ground.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Coming up into the basin, stay somewhat LEFT to arrive at the notch at the base of the west ridge — that notch, not the ridge crest above it, is the reference point. From the notch, traverse along ledges for about 100 feet to reach the foot of a shallow gully that runs up and LEFT to gain the ridge crest, and that gully is where the climbing begins. Three rope lengths or so above it you arrive at a sandy area at the top of the southwest gully, which is the natural regrouping spot and confirms you are on line. If you rope up at the notch itself without making the ledge traverse, you are starting one feature too early.
hazards: loose rock throughout the ridge and on the descent gullies
long day relative to the short approach
route-finding on the descent — the direct-looking line down cliffs out

approach_variants.name: State Creek approach, then over the rib into the east basin
approach_variants.season: Soon after SR-20 reopens — typically Apr-May
approach_variants.notes:
This route is on the EAST face of Cutthroat Peak, and the approach is the South Buttress approach with an extra step. Park in the long pullout on the north side of SR-20 about a mile and a half west of Washington Pass, find the cairned climbers' track leaving the east end of it, drop through timber and cross State Creek, then climb toward the basin below the south side of the peak.

From there, cross OVER the rib that extends south from the South Buttress and drop into the basin EAST of Cutthroat Peak. That crossing is what separates this approach from the rock-route approach, and it is the part with no boot path.

The route is in condition for a short window right after the highway opens each spring, usually April or May. SR-20 across Washington Pass is gated all winter — typically closing late November or early December and reopening mid-April to early May — so the season starts when the gate does.
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the east basin the objective is the large couloir splitting the East Face; it is the dominant gully feature on that aspect and there is no ambiguity about which one it is once you are in the correct basin. The navigational error to avoid is a basin error, not a gully error — if you are looking up at the south-facing buttresses and gullies that the rock routes use, you have not crossed the rib yet. The couloir begins as snow or névé and climbs several hundred feet before the first proper ice pitch, so the transition from approach to route is gradual; treat the base of the continuous snow in the couloir as the start.
hazards: east-facing slopes take sun for most of the day — serious avalanche and wet-slide concern, and a strong argument for a very early start
no established path across the rib into the east basin
State Creek crossing in spring melt
short seasonal window tied to the SR-20 opening

approach_variants.name: State Creek approach, then over the rib into the east basin
approach_variants.season: Soon after SR-20 reopens — typically Apr-May
approach_variants.notes:
Same walk-in as the South Buttress rock routes: the long pullout on the north side of SR-20 about a mile and a half west of Washington Pass, the cairned climbers' track from its east end, down through timber, across State Creek, and up toward the basin south of the peak. Then cross the rib running south from the South Buttress and drop into the basin EAST of Cutthroat Peak.

The window is set by the highway. SR-20 over Washington Pass is closed each winter, usually from late November or early December until mid-April to early May, and this route is climbed as soon as practical after it reopens.
approach_variants.baseFinding: The route takes the big couloir on the East Face, so being in the correct basin is the whole navigation problem — from the east basin the couloir is the obvious dominant gully and cannot be confused with anything else. If the buttresses above you face south and you can see the entry gullies used by the rock routes, you are still on the wrong side of the rib. The climbing starts on snow or névé at the foot of the couloir and steepens gradually to the first ice pitch, so there is no distinct rock feature marking a start.
hazards: east aspect in the sun most of the day — avalanche and wet-slide danger
unmarked crossing of the rib into the east basin
creek crossing in spring flow
very short season tied to the highway reopening

approach_variants.name: Burgundy Col in a single push
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the pullout on SR-20 near milepost 166, roughly four miles east of Washington Pass and looking straight across the valley at Silver Star Mountain. There is no numbered Forest Service trail here — the whole thing is an established boot path.

Scramble down the embankment past cairns. The first stretch is loose, scree-covered talus before it settles into a proper path. Cross Early Winters Creek on one of the logs; the logjam shifts year to year, so look up and down stream for the best one, and expect a cold, pushy ford in early season.

On the far bank the path winds through forest for about a quarter of a mile, then turns straight uphill between two small creeks and climbs relentlessly. At about 6,460 ft the angle relents at a broad flat bench — big enough for a dozen tents and the obvious rest stop.

Above the bench the path climbs and traverses loose scree gullies before a final cairned stretch of very unstable scree over slab to Burgundy Col at about 7,770 ft, the notch between Burgundy Spire and Paisano Pinnacle. That is roughly 3,700 ft above the creek. That last scree is worse on the way down than the way up.
approach_variants.baseFinding: The col is the destination and the route starts essentially straight off it. Burgundy Col is a narrow notch with Burgundy Spire on one side and Paisano Pinnacle on the other, and once you are stood in it the first pitch is directly above and visually obvious — the North Face rises immediately from the col rather than requiring any traverse along the base. If you have to walk any distance from the notch to find a start, you are at the wrong notch. Confirmation from the col: the Silver Star Glacier lies below on the far (east) side, so a col that drops onto a glacier behind you is the right one.
hazards: Early Winters Creek crossing — logs shift, and the ford is cold and swift in early season
extremely unstable ball-bearing scree over slab on the final stretch to the col — this is the section that kicks rocks onto whoever is below, so travel close together
loose talus on the initial drop from the highway
very large gain for a day trip; most parties camp

approach_variants.name: Camp at the 6,460 ft bench
approach_variants.notes:
The usual way this is done. Walk the same line from the milepost 166 pullout — down the loose talus embankment, across Early Winters Creek on logs, through the forest and then steeply up between the two small creeks — and stop at the broad flat bench at about 6,460 ft, which holds a dozen or more tents and is the natural halfway point. There is usually a seasonal trickle or snowmelt nearby.

Next morning you carry only what you need for the col and the route, which makes the loose scree above the bench substantially less unpleasant. Reckon on the bench being the last flat ground and the last water.
approach_variants.baseFinding: From camp, the route to the col climbs and traverses scree gullies with cairns on the final stretch. Aim for the narrow notch with Burgundy Spire on your left and Paisano Pinnacle on your right; the first pitch of the North Face rises directly out of it. Do not take the obvious direct gully that appears to lead straight to the col — it is loose and exposed. The path goes up the gully above camp and then makes a rising traverse right beneath the cliffs on heather-covered slabs into the col.
hazards: the direct-looking gully to the col is the wrong line — loose and exposed
loose scree over slab on the traverse into the col
no water above the bench
rockfall onto parties below on the final approach

approach_variants.name: Burgundy Col and the glacier, in a day
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the pullout on SR-20 near milepost 166, about four miles east of Washington Pass. Drop the embankment — around 150 to 200 feet down loose ground — to Early Winters Creek and cross on a log; the logjam moves year to year, so scout, and be ready to ford in early-season high water.

On the far side pick up the well-defined climbers' path up the timbered rib on the west side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. It climbs steeply and almost without switchbacks. Treat the creek as your last reliable water.

Around 6,000 to 6,400 ft the grade eases at the bench, an open larch and heather shelf with established campsites. Above it, continue toward Burgundy Col — roughly 3,500 ft of gain from the highway to the col.

Do not take the obvious direct gully to the col: it is loose and exposed. Stay left, follow the trail up the gully directly above the camp area, and near its head make an ascending traverse right under the cliffs on heather-covered slabs into the col at about 7,770 ft.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The col is not the start of the climbing — the glacier is on the FAR side of it. From Burgundy Col, descend roughly 200 feet of steep snow down the east side onto the Silver Star Glacier; that descent is the moment the route begins, and parties rope up at the edge of the glacier below it. Head east, climb to the flat top of a spur ridge, then traverse east onto the main body of the glacier and ascend south to the saddle just west of the summit.

The finish is where people get it wrong. From that saddle the summit is a short scramble east, but only on one line: look for an easy RAMP about 40 feet below the summit. Take it and the summit is class 3 to 4. Miss it and you end up on a short pitch of low fifth class instead. In poor visibility, work generally left off the saddle and hunt for the ramp rather than committing to the first steep line you meet.
hazards: Early Winters Creek crossing — log can be wet or washed out, ford is cold and fast in early season
steep eroding brushy tread in the timber, easy to lose
loose ball-bearing rock on the final gully and traverse into the col
crevasses on the upper glacier, more open late season
the return traverse drops BELOW the elevation of Burgundy Col, so the descent includes a couple of hundred feet of reclimbing steep snow back up to the notch — parties are caught out by this
descending the loose ground below the col has taken parties three hours or more

approach_variants.name: Camp at the bench, summit the second day
approach_variants.notes:
The same line from the milepost 166 pullout, broken at the open bench at roughly 6,000 to 6,400 ft where the climbers' path first eases. There are several established sites there, usually with a seasonal trickle or snowmelt nearby, and it is the standard overnight for this peak.

Camping here means you cross the glacier on firm morning snow and are back over the col before the afternoon softening, which matters given the reclimb to the col on the way out.
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the bench, follow the trail up the gully directly above camp — not the obvious direct gully toward the col, which is loose and exposed — and near its head traverse rightward under the cliffs on heather slabs into Burgundy Col. Then drop about 200 feet of steep snow off the east side of the col onto the Silver Star Glacier and rope up at the glacier's edge. The col has Burgundy Spire on one side and Paisano Pinnacle on the other, and a glacier behind it; if there is no glacier on the far side, it is not the col.
hazards: the direct gully to the col is the wrong line — loose and exposed
no water above the bench once the seasonal trickle dries
crevasses on the upper glacier
the reclimb back up to Burgundy Col at the end of the day
